claims.text: The superconducting transition temperature in high-entropy superconducting alloys is governed by the degree of chemical disorder.
Chemical disorder modifies local lattice distortions.
Chemical disorder modifies the electronic density of states.
Changes in local lattice distortions and electronic density of states modulate electron-phonon coupling.
A moderate increase in chemical disorder initially enhances Tc.
Excessive chemical disorder suppresses superconductivity by increasing electron scattering.
The proposed starting alloy is a disordered, single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 atomic percent each.
The proposed starting alloy exhibits a baseline superconducting transition temperature.
Varying the concentration of one constituent while keeping the overall electron count nearly constant modifies the degree of chemical disorder.
Local chemical disorder influences vibrational modes relevant to electron-phonon coupling.
A moderate increase in chemical disorder enhances the density of states at the Fermi level.
A moderate increase in chemical disorder strengthens electron-phonon coupling.
An enhanced density of states at the Fermi level and stronger electron-phonon coupling raise Tc.
Beyond an optimum disorder level, increased electron scattering counteracts the proposed benefits of disorder and lowers Tc.
Relative to the baseline alloy, samples with a moderate increase in chemical disorder will have a higher Tc.
Relative to the baseline alloy, samples with excessive chemical disorder will have a lower Tc.
The proposed relationship applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase disordered solid solution with nearly constant electron count.
Phase separation, chemical ordering, or additional electronic interactions may invalidate the proposed disorder-Tc relationship.
